L0@P0: RESTler: Stateful REST API Fuzzing
L1@P0: Vaggelis Atlidakis∗
L2@P0: Columbia University
L3@P0: Patrice Godefroid
L4@P0: Microsoft Research
L5@P0: Marina Polishchuk
L6@P0: Microsoft Research
L7@P0: Abstract—This paper introduces RESTler, the first stateful
L8@P0: REST API fuzzer. RESTler analyzes the API specification of
L9@P0: a cloud service and generates sequences of requests that automatically test the service through its API. RESTler generates
L10@P0: test sequences by (1) inferring producer-consumer dependencies
L11@P0: among request types declared in the specification (e.g., inferring
L12@P0: that “a request B should be executed after request A” because
L13@P0: B takes as an input a resource-id x produced by A) and by
L14@P0: (2) analyzing dynamic feedback from responses observed during
L15@P0: prior test executions in order to generate new tests (e.g., learning
L16@P0: that “a request C after a request sequence A;B is refused by the
L17@P0: service” and therefore avoiding this combination in the future).
L18@P0: We present experimental results showing that these two
L19@P0: techniques are necessary to thoroughly exercise a service under
L20@P0: test while pruning the large search space of possible request
L21@P0: sequences. We used RESTler to test GitLab, an open-source Git
L22@P0: service, as well as several Microsoft Azure and Office365 cloud
L23@P0: services. RESTler found 28 bugs in GitLab and several bugs in
L24@P0: each of the Azure and Office365 cloud services tested so far. These
L25@P0: bugs have been confirmed and fixed by the service owners.
L26@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L27@P0: Over the last decade, we have seen an explosion in cloud
L28@P0: services for hosting software applications (Software-as-aService), for building distributed services and data processing
L29@P0: (Platform-as-a-Service), and for providing general computing
L30@P0: infrastructure (Infrastructure-as-a-Service). Today, most cloud
L31@P0: services, such as those provided by Amazon Web Services
L32@P0: (AWS) [2] and Microsoft Azure [29], are programmatically accessed through REST APIs [11] by third-party applications [1]
L33@P0: and other services [31]. Meanwhile, Swagger (recently renamed OpenAPI) [40] has arguably become the most popular
L34@P0: interface-description language for REST APIs. A Swagger
L35@P0: specification describes how to access a cloud service through
L36@P0: its REST API, including what requests the service can handle,
L37@P0: what responses may be received, and the response format.
L38@P0: Tools for automatically testing cloud services via their
L39@P0: REST APIs and checking whether those services are reliable
L40@P0: and secure are still in their infancy. The most sophisticated
L41@P0: testing tools currently available for REST APIs capture live
L42@P0: API traffic, and then parse, fuzz and replay the traffic with the
L43@P0: hope of finding bugs [4], [34], [7], [41], [3]. Many of these
L44@P0: tools were born as extensions of more established website
L45@P0: testing and scanning tools (see Section VIII). Since these
L46@P0: REST API testing tools are all recent and not yet widely used,
L47@P0: it is still largely unknown how effective they are in finding
L48@P0: bugs and how security-critical those bugs are.
L49@P0: In this paper, we introduce RESTler, the first automatic
L50@P0: stateful REST API fuzzing tool. Fuzzing [39] means automatic
L51@P0: ∗The work of this author was mostly done at Microsoft Research.
L52@P0: test generation and execution with the goal of finding security
L53@P0: vulnerabilities. Unlike other REST API testing tools, RESTler
L54@P0: performs a lightweight static analysis of an entire Swagger
L55@P0: specification, and then generates and executes tests that exercise the corresponding cloud service in a stateful manner. By
L56@P0: stateful, we mean that RESTler attempts to explore service
L57@P0: states that are reachable only using sequences of multiple
L58@P0: requests. With RESTler, each test is defined as a sequence
L59@P0: of requests and responses. RESTler generates tests by:
L60@P0: 1) inferring dependencies among request types declared in
L61@P0: the Swagger specification (e.g., inferring that a resource
L62@P0: included in the response of a request A is necessary as
L63@P0: input argument of another request B, and therefore that
L64@P0: A should be executed before B), and by
L65@P0: 2) analyzing dynamic feedback from responses observed
L66@P0: during prior test executions in order to generate new tests
L67@P0: (e.g., learning that “a request C after a request sequence
L68@P0: A;B is refused by the service” and therefore avoiding
L69@P0: this combination in the future).

L11: Authors:【6†Zheng Guo】, 【7†David Cao】, 【8†Davin Tjong】, 【9†Jean Yang】, 【10†Cole Schlesinger】, 【11†Nadia Polikarpova】

L16: > Abstract:With the rise of software-as-a-service and microservice architectures, RESTful APIs are now ubiquitous in mobile and web applications. A service can have tens or hundreds of API methods, making it a challenge for programmers to find the right combination of methods to solve their task.
L17: > We present APIphany, a component-based synthesizer for programs that compose calls to RESTful APIs. The main innovation behind APIphany is the use of precise semantic types, both to specify user intent and to direct the search.
L18: APIphany contributes three novel mechanisms to overcome challenges in adapting component-based synthesis to the REST domain: (1) a type inference algorithm for augmenting REST specifications with semantic types; (2) an efficient synthesis technique for "wrangling" semi-structured data, which is commonly required in working with RESTful APIs; and (3) a new form of simulated execution to avoid executing APIs calls during synthesis.
L19: We evaluate APIphany on three real-world APIs and 32 tasks extracted from GitHub repositories and StackOverflow. In our experiments, APIphany found correct solutions to 29 tasks, with 23 of them reported among top ten synthesis results.

L443: Partial observation aims to improve the modeling capabilities. While a system may contain numerous variables, the controller usually has access to only a few of them [【54†19】]. In this section, we study an extension of $\mathrm{𝖢𝖫𝖳𝖫}$ that features partial observation: we split our set of input variables into two subsets, public (visible) inputs ${𝕀}_{v}$ and private (hidden) inputs ${𝕀}_{h}$.
L444: ###### Example 29.
L445: To illustrate this setting, consider an environment that, at each turn, outputs two public values ${\text{in}}_{1},{\text{in}}_{2}$. One of them must be equal to some private (hidden) variable t (target), that the controller aims at identifying infinitely often, using some variable g (guess) that it outputs at each turn. Such a setting can be captured as follows. Let ${𝕀}_{v}=\{{\text{in}}_{1},{\text{in}}_{2}\}$, ${𝕀}_{h}=\{\text{t}\}$ and $𝕆=\{\text{g}\}$ and consider the following formula:
L446:  | $$\mathrm{\Phi }=G\left(\underset{i\in \{1,2\}}{\bigvee }{\text{in}}_{i}^{(0)}={\text{t}}^{(0)}\right)\Rightarrow GF\left({\text{g}}^{(0)}={\text{t}}^{(0)}\right)$$  |
L447: As $𝔻$ is infinite and the way t alternates between ${\text{in}}_{1}$ and ${\text{in}}_{2}$ is arbitrary, this formula is not realizable. Indeed, for any strategy of the controller (output ${\text{in}}_{1}$, resp. ${\text{in}}_{2}$), the environment can take the opposite decision (set $\text{t}={\text{in}}_{2}$, resp. $\text{t}={\text{in}}_{1}$). However, if we assume a periodic behavior of the environment, then we obtain the following formula (here with period $p$):
L448:  | $${\mathrm{\Phi }}_{\text{per}}=\left(G\left({\text{t}}^{(0)}={\text{t}}^{(p)}\right)\wedge G\left(\underset{i\in \{1,2\}}{\bigvee }{\text{in}}_{i}^{(0)}={\text{t}}^{(0)}\right)\right)\Rightarrow GF\left({\text{g}}^{(0)}={\text{t}}^{(0)}\right)$$  |

L141: ###### Definition 3.1 (Deducibility).
L142: 
L143: Let $\phi$ be finite set of deductions facts. We say that $M$ is a recipe of $t$ in $\phi$, written $M\rhd_{\phi}t$, if there exist a (public, ground, non-necessarily linear) $n$-ary context $C$ and some deduction facts $M_{1}\rhd t_{1}$, …, $M_{n}\rhd t_{n}$ in $\phi$ such that $M=C[M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}]$ and $t=C[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}]$. In that case, we say that $t$ is syntactically deducible from $\phi$, also written $\phi\vdash t$.
L144: We say that $M$ is a recipe of $t$ in $\phi$ modulo $\mathsf{E}$, written $M\rhd^{\mathsf{E}}_{\phi}t$, if there exists a term $t^{\prime}$ such that $M\rhd_{\phi}t^{\prime}$ and $t^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{E}}t$. In that case, we say that $t$ is deducible from $\phi$ modulo $\mathsf{E}$, written $\phi\vdash_{\mathsf{E}}t$.
L145: We note that $M\rhd_{\varphi}t$ is equivalent to $M\varphi=t$ when $\varphi$ is an initial frame and when $t$ (or equivalently $M$) is ground. We also note that in the case of a frame $\varphi$, since our contexts $C$ are ground and public, $M\rhd_{\varphi}t$ implies $\operatorname{var}(M,t)=\emptyset$ and $\operatorname{par}(M)\subseteq\operatorname{par}(\varphi)$.
L146: ###### Example 3.2.
L147: Consider the equational theory $\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}$ described in Example 【55†2.1】. Let $\varphi_{0}=\{\mathsf{w}_{1}\rhd\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{0},\mathsf{k}),\mathsf{w}_{2}\rhd\mathsf{k}\}$ where $\mathsf{c}_{0}$ is a public constant and $\mathsf{k}$ is a private constant. We have that $\varphi_{0}$ is a set of deduction facts. Since, these facts are ground, $\varphi_{0}$ is actually a frame. Moreover, this frame is initial.
L148: We have that $\langle\mathsf{w}_{2},\mathsf{w}_{2}\rangle\rhd_{\varphi_{0}}\langle\mathsf{k},\mathsf{k}\rangle$, $\mathsf{c}_{0}\rhd_{\varphi_{0}}\mathsf{c}_{0}$, and $\mathsf{dec}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\rhd_{\varphi_{0}}^{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}\mathsf{c}_{0}$.
L149: ### 3.2 Static equivalence, visible equations
L150: Deducibility does not always suffice for expressing the knowledge of an attacker. In particular, it does not account for the partial information that an attacker may obtain about secrets. Sometimes, the attacker can deduce exactly the same set of terms from two different frames but he could still be able to tell the difference between these two frames. This issue motivates the study of visible equations and static equivalence (see [【36†3】]), defined as follows.
L151: ###### Definition 3.3 (Static equivalence).
L152: 
L153: Let $\varphi$ be an initial frame. The set of visible equations of $\varphi$ modulo $\mathsf{E}$ is defined as
L154: 
L155:  | $$\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi)=\{M\bowtie N\;|\;M,N\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}[\operatorname{dom}(\varphi)],\;M\varphi=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi\}$$  |
L156: where $\bowtie$ is a dedicated commutative symbol. Two initial frames $\varphi_{1}$ and $\varphi_{2}$ with the same domain are statically equivalent modulo $\mathsf{E}$, written ${\varphi_{1}\approx_{\mathsf{E}}\varphi_{2}}$, if their sets of visible equations are equal, i.e. $\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{1})=\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{2})$.
L157: This definition is in line with static equivalence in the applied pi calculus [【36†3】] where bounds names would be replaced by free private constants.
L158: ###### Example 3.4.
L159: 
L160: Consider again the equational theory $\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}$ given in Example 【55†2.1】. Let $\varphi_{0}=\{\mathsf{w}_{1}\rhd\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{0},\mathsf{k}),\;\mathsf{w}_{2}\rhd\mathsf{k}\}$ and $\varphi_{1}=\{\mathsf{w}_{1}\rhd\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{1},\mathsf{k}),\;\mathsf{w}_{2}\rhd\mathsf{k}\}$ where $\mathsf{c}_{0}$, $\mathsf{c}_{1}$ are public constants and $\mathsf{k}$ is a private constant. We have that:
L161: 
L162:   * •
L163: $(\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{0},\mathsf{w}_{2})\bowtie\mathsf{w}_{1})\in\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}(\varphi_{0})$, and
L164: 
L165:   * •
L166: 
L167: $(\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{0},\mathsf{w}_{2})\bowtie\mathsf{w}_{1})\not\in\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}(\varphi_{1})$.
L168: Hence, $\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}(\varphi_{0})\neq\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}(\varphi_{1})$ and the two frames $\varphi_{0}$ and $\varphi_{1}$ are not statically equivalent. However, it can be shown that $\{\mathsf{w}_{1}\rhd\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{0},\mathsf{k})\}\approx_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}\{\mathsf{w}_{1}\rhd\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{1},\mathsf{k})\}$.
L169: For the purpose of finitely describing the set of visible equations $\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi)$ of an initial frame, we introduce quantified equations of the form $\forall z_{1},\ldots,z_{q}.M\bowtie N$ where $z_{1}$, …, $z_{q}\in\mathcal{X}$, $q\geq 0$ and $\operatorname{var}(M,N)\subseteq\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{q}\}$.
L170: In what follows, finite sets of quantified equations are denoted $\Psi$, $\Psi_{0}$,… We write $\Psi\models M\bowtie N$ when the ground equation $M\bowtie N$ is a consequence of $\Psi$ in the usual, first-order logics with equality axioms for the relation $\bowtie$ (that is, reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity and compatibility with symbols in $\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}$). When no confusion arises, we may refer to quantified equations simply as equations.
L171: As usual, quantified equations are considered up to renaming of bound variables.
